title: Uber and Pony.ai plan to bring 2,000 robotaxis to Europe
slides: Uber's robotaxis hit Europe—but will Pony.ai's tech work?
Two thousand self-driving cars are planned by 2026.
Most will operate in Germany, yet regulators remain silent.
Your Uber rides could soon be driverless—at lower cost.
Test one in Stuttgart now; decisions will shape your future.
thread_text:
1. Why Stuttgart might fail

Pony.ai's tech has never been tested in European traffic, yet Uber is betting on it for 2,000 robotaxis.

2. The 2026 deadline

Those 2,000 cars target most of their fleet in Germany, where regulators haven't even approved the tech.

3. Silent regulators, big risks

While the government stays quiet, Uber's lower costs could cut fares—and safety oversights could follow.

4. Your ride goes driverless

The app will offer you a robotaxi in Stuttgart soon; costs drop, but who checks the brakes?

5. Test one today

Book a ride in Stuttgart and see if you trust the empty driver's seat. Would you?

instagram.caption:
Stuttgart’s streets are about to get 2,000 self-driving Ubers, and the company is betting Pony.ai’s tech will handle European traffic. 🚗

The catch? Most of those robotaxis head to Germany, where regulators haven’t approved the system yet. And Pony.ai has never driven in European conditions. Lower fares might arrive—but nobody’s officially checking the brakes.

For you, this means your Uber app will soon offer a driverless ride in Stuttgart. If you’re a creator or business owner, expect cheaper transport logistics—but also a new layer of uncertainty about safety standards in your city.

Would you book that empty driver’s seat before regulators speak up? 🛑

Test one in Stuttgart and decide yourself.

Uber and Pony.ai target most of their fleet in Germany, where regulators haven't even approved the technology. The deadline looms, but questions remain.
With government silence, Uber's lower costs could cut fares—but safety oversights might follow. The tech is untested in European conditions.
Uber will soon offer robotaxis in Stuttgart, cutting costs. But without clear oversight, who ensures the vehicle is safe before you get in?
